## Where the AI surveys agree with the polls {#sources}

AI surveys and polls generally agree on which states favour each party but they often differ on the size of the lead. Across 33 states with polling data their estimates have a correlation of 0.85 and agree on the leading party in 26 states. Overall the AI estimates are about 7.2 percentage points more Republican than the polls. 

The differences are particularly large in Oklahoma, Idaho, Tennessee and South Dakota where the AI is much more Republican than the polls. New Hampshire shows the opposite pattern with the AI favouring the Democrat while the polls favour the Republican. We correct these differences before using the AI estimates in the forecast and give more weight to polls where they are available.

```{python}
#| label: fig-silicon-polls
#| fig-cap: "AI-survey margin (Methods A and B averaged, before correction) against the poll average, one dot per state with polls. On the solid line they agree; the dashed line is the fitted correction used in the forecast."
#| fig-alt: "Scatter plot with one dot per state, the poll average on the horizontal axis and the AI-survey margin on the vertical axis. Most dots sit below the diagonal, meaning the AI surveys lean more Republican than the polls."
P.chart("silicon_vs_polls", scale=0.75)
```

```{python}
#| label: fig-sources
#| fig-cap: "What each source says about every race, beside the forecast that combines them. The AI surveys are shown after the correction in the figure above."
#| fig-alt: "For each of the 36 races, a row showing the past-results estimate (grey square), the corrected AI survey (gold triangle), the poll average (white diamond) and the final forecast (blue or red dot)."
P.chart("sources")
```

### Asking the model for a forecast instead

We also asked the same three models to function as forecasters (Method C) and 
compared their answers to the polls in the 33 states that have them (@tbl-sources). 
Method C favoured the same candidate as the polls in 30 of the 33 states, 
compared to 26 for the raw AI surveys. It was 10.3 points from the poll margin 
on average (vs 12.4 for the raw AI surveys and 6.2 after their correction). 
Like the AI surveys, it leaned Republican (9.3 points on average). Its worst 
performances were in Vermont (R+27.7 vs R+2.5 in the polls), Nebraska (R+27.2 vs R+3.2), 
Oklahoma (R+26.3 vs R+4.8) and Rhode Island, where it had the Democrat 
only 19 points ahead of the Republican (vs 48 in the polls). We report Method C 
purely for comparison and avoid including it in the forecast. This is because a model asked to 
forecast is likely to be drawing on the polls, the ratings and past results it 
has already seen, which are sources the forecast already uses.

```{python}
#| label: tbl-sources
#| tbl-cap: "Every source's margin for every race. Methods A and B are the AI surveys before correction; Method C is the models asked as forecasters, averaged over models, repeats and days, and not used in the forecast."
P.tbl_sources()
```
